newsitem.title: FRANCE: Nuclear train back on French tracks after accident.
newsitem.headline: Nuclear train back on French tracks after accident.

text.p: A train carrying spent nuclear fuel which derailed in eastern France resumed its voyage to Dunkirk and Britain on Wednesday after 36 hours of repairs and safety tests, French officials said.
"The train left Apach at 5.55 p.m. (1655 GMT)," a spokeswoman for the prefect's office for France's Moselle department said by telephone from Metz.

The train was allowed to go on its way after safety inspectors determined there had been no radiation leaks from the three wagons which jumped the tracks, each of them loaded with 6.5 tonnes of spent nuclear fuel, she said.
Work went on through the night to put the wagons upright and on the rails.
The mishap occurred early on Tuesday when the convoy, bound for Britain from Germany, was derailed at Apach.

Germany's opposition Greens party said the accident was one of a series of recent nuclear mishaps including an incident at Britain's Sellafield plant on Sunday in which six workers were contaminated by radioactive dust.
The convoy was carrying 18 spent fuel elements from the Lingen power station in Lower Saxony, according to the Lower Saxony environment ministry.
The Metz prefect's office said the convoy belonged to British Nuclear Fuels Plc and was on its way to Dunkirk for shipment to Britain by ferry.
The Saarland state Interior Ministry said the shipment was on its way to the reprocessing plant at Sellafield in northwestern England.

The French Institute for Nuclear Protection and Safety (IPSN) said shipments of spent nuclear fuel were not unusual in France. It said some 450 fuel shipments took place every year, with half being moved by train, 40 percent by boat and 10 percent by truck.

Between 1978 and 1995, there have been 25 accidents or incidents during the shipment of spent nuclear fuel, it said, 15 involving rail transport, nine involving transport by truck and one involving transport by sea.
In all of these, the cargo itself was affected just twice: once in a traffic accident in June 1987 and once during the unloading of a shipment in the port of Cherbourg in December 1991.

In the traffic accident, the nuclear container fell off a lorry into a roadside ditch. In the Cherbourg accident, a chain broke during unloading, causing a nuclear container to fall onto the ship's deck.
In neither case were there any radiation leaks, the IPSN said.
Tuesday's derailment occurred just outside the village of Apach, on a railway line running alongside the Moselle river.
The spot where the train ran off the rails was about 500 metres (yards) from France's border with Germany, officials said.
